cards.meaning: Lying on your back with your face pointing upward.
cards.nuance: Formal and more often used in writing. It can also describe someone as passive or overly accepting.

uses.sentence: The patient remained supine while the nurse checked his breathing.
uses.tip: Common in medical and first-aid descriptions.

uses.where: Rooftop party · relaxing on a lounger
uses.sentence: She lay supine on the lounger, enjoying the warm evening breeze.
uses.tip: Use it for a deliberately elegant or humorous description of lying face-up.

uses.sentence: The essay criticises the supine acceptance of rules that no longer serve the public.
uses.tip: This figurative use is formal and sounds slightly critical.

origin.summary: From Latin supinus, meaning ‘lying on the back’. Its deeper pre-Latin origin is uncertain.

timeline.text: Supinus means ‘lying on the back’, with the face turned upward.
The word begins appearing in English in medical and descriptive writing.
It is mainly used formally for a face-up position or passive behaviour.

cards.pitfall: Do not confuse it with ‘subline’ or ‘sub-line’, which can mean a smaller line of text.

cards.meaning: Easily influenced, harmed, or affected by something.
cards.nuance: Often describes someone or something that is vulnerable to a particular influence, danger, or condition. It can sound more formal than “vulnerable” or “prone to.”

uses.where: Security review · evaluating a new tool
uses.sentence: The system is susceptible to attack if the old login method remains enabled.
uses.tip: Use it to describe a specific weakness or risk.

uses.sentence: She was susceptible to the idea once she saw how much fun the group was having.
uses.tip: Use it for someone who is easily swayed by an appealing idea.

uses.sentence: People with weakened immune systems are more susceptible to certain infections.
uses.tip: In formal writing, it often takes the preposition “to.”

origin.summary: From Latin susceptibilis, meaning “able to receive or be affected,” based on suscipere, “to take upon oneself, receive, or feel.”

timeline.text: Suscipere means “to take upon oneself, receive, or feel,” and gives us susceptible.
The word enters English with meanings connected with receiving, being affected, or being exposed.
It mainly means easily influenced, harmed, or affected by something.

cards.pitfall: Use “susceptible to” for a risk or influence; don’t confuse it with “susceptive,” which means suspicious.

cards.register: Common in medicine, work and formal writing
cards.meaning: Showing that a problem or condition exists, especially as a sign of a larger issue.
cards.nuance: In medicine, it means showing signs of a disease or condition. More broadly, “symptomatic of” suggests that something is a typical sign of a deeper problem.

uses.sentence: The missed handoffs are symptomatic of a wider problem with unclear ownership.
uses.tip: Use “symptomatic of” when connecting an immediate issue to its underlying cause.

uses.sentence: His constant checking of his phone is symptomatic of how anxious he feels when we go out.
uses.tip: It can describe a personal sign that points to a broader emotional situation.

uses.sentence: Falling sales are symptomatic of weak demand rather than a problem with the product itself.
uses.tip: It sounds more analytical than “a sign of” and suits reports, reviews and diagnosis.

origin.summary: From Greek symptomatikos, meaning “showing symptoms,” which comes from symptōma, “a sign or indication” of illness.

timeline.text: Symptōma develops as a medical term for a sign or indication of illness.
The word enters English in medical writing as a noun meaning a sign of disease.
The adjective comes to mean showing symptoms, then extends to revealing a larger problem.

cards.pitfall: Someone or something can be “symptomatic” in the medical sense without being the cause of the condition. Also, use “symptomatic of” when naming what the symptom indicates.

cards.register: Common in personal, health and workplace contexts
cards.meaning: Treatment intended to help someone improve their physical or mental health.
cards.nuance: It can refer to a formal medical or psychological treatment, or, informally, to a conversation or activity that helps someone feel better.

uses.sentence: Regular therapy sessions have helped her manage stress while working through a busy project.
uses.tip: Use it for structured support from a mental health professional, especially when workplace stress is affecting someone.

uses.where: Conversation with a friend · offering support
uses.sentence: Talking to my friend was a form of therapy, even though neither of us called it that.
uses.tip: In social conversation, it can sound light or informal when you mean an emotional release rather than medical treatment.

uses.sentence: The company offers therapy referrals and confidential appointments for employees who need extra support.
uses.tip: It sounds professional and clear when describing a service, programme or range of treatment options.

origin.summary: From Greek therapeia, meaning attendance or service, associated with caring for someone and helping them recover. The medical sense became established in English during the 18th century.

timeline.text: therapeia meant attendance, service or care, especially the care given to the sick.
The word appears in English with medical and healing-related meanings.
Its modern medical and psychological meanings become established.
It is used for medical care, psychological treatment and, informally, emotional support.

cards.pitfall: Therapy usually describes a process or field of treatment; a therapist is the person who provides it.

cards.meaning: Poisonous or extremely harmful, including when describing relationships, behaviours or environments.
cards.nuance: For substances, it means capable of causing illness or death. For people, workplaces or online exchanges, it suggests persistent damage to wellbeing or morale.

uses.sentence: Constant criticism created a toxic environment, so we need to change how feedback is handled.
uses.tip: Use it to describe serious, ongoing harm rather than ordinary disagreement.

uses.where: Dinner with friends · discussing a friendship
uses.sentence: The relationship became toxic, and leaving felt healthier than trying to fix it.
uses.tip: This figurative use is common when a friendship or interaction regularly damages your confidence or peace of mind.

uses.where: Email to a colleague · setting boundaries
uses.sentence: I’m willing to continue the project, but I won’t accept a toxic communication style.
uses.tip: Pair it with environment, behaviour, culture or waste to make your point clear.

origin.summary: From Greek toxikon, meaning poison or poison-related, which comes from toxikos, meaning poisonous.

timeline.text: Toxikon meant poison and was linked to toxos, the bow used to shoot poisoned arrows.
The word enters English in medical contexts.
Figurative uses develop for harmful relationships, cultures and communication.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use toxic for every unpleasant person or difficult situation; it suggests serious or persistent harm.

cards.meaning: A strong feeling that you or the world around you is spinning, often causing you to lose balance.
cards.nuance: Vertigo is more intense than ordinary dizziness and is often used for a spinning sensation caused by balance problems. In less formal writing, it can describe confusion or disorientation caused by a sudden change.

uses.sentence: When the budget was cut, I felt a moment of vertigo as the team tried to decide what to keep.
uses.tip: Use it metaphorically when a situation suddenly leaves you feeling unsure which way to go.

uses.sentence: I nearly dropped my drink when I looked over the edge; that rooftop gave me serious vertigo.
uses.tip: It often works well as an adjective before a noun such as vertigo, dizziness or episodes.

uses.sentence: The patient reported brief episodes of vertigo when turning her head.
uses.tip: Choose vertigo when the spinning sensation is the main symptom, rather than general light-headedness.

origin.summary: From Latin vertigo, meaning a turn or spinning motion, based on vertere, “to turn.” The medical sense developed through later descriptions of dizziness and loss of balance.

timeline.text: Vertigo refers to a turning or spinning motion and comes from vertere, “to turn.”
The word appears in medical writing for dizziness and the spinning sensation.
It mainly names a specific spinning sensation and can also suggest emotional or situational disorientation.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use vertigo as a general synonym for every dizzy feeling; it usually suggests a pronounced spinning sensation or loss of balance.

cards.meaning: Extremely harmful, severe, or capable of spreading quickly, especially when describing a disease, substance, or hostile attack.
cards.nuance: In medicine and biology, it describes something intensely dangerous or rapidly spreading. Figuratively, it can describe vicious language or attacks.

uses.sentence: The security team called the script virulent because it spread rapidly through shared drives.
uses.tip: Common in technical discussions about diseases, toxins, viruses, and malicious software.

uses.sentence: One guest’s comment was so virulent that everyone else went quiet.
uses.tip: Use it figuratively for hostile or vicious speech that has a strong effect.

uses.sentence: The report describes the strain as highly virulent, with cases developing within days.
uses.tip: Pairs naturally with words such as disease, strain, strain, pathogen, and virus.

origin.summary: From Latin virulentus, meaning ‘poisonous’ or ‘full of poison’, which developed from virus, an old word for poison or harmful material.

timeline.text: Virulentus means ‘poisonous’ and is related to virus, ‘poison’ or ‘harmful material’.
The word enters English with meanings connected with poison and disease.
It is used mainly for severe disease or harmful material, and figuratively for vicious attacks.

cards.pitfall: Don’t use it merely as a stronger form of harmful; it suggests great severity, rapid spread, or an especially intense effect.

cards.meaning: Pale and weak, especially because of illness, exhaustion or worry.
cards.nuance: It creates a sombre, often old-fashioned atmosphere. It is stronger and more emotional than simply saying someone looks pale.

uses.sentence: By late afternoon, even the most energetic employees had turned wan after another round of changes.
uses.tip: Useful in serious, literary writing about exhaustion or emotional strain.

uses.sentence: Her wan face showed that the weekend had not been restful.
uses.tip: It sounds caring but slightly dramatic, so use it mainly when the mood is serious.

uses.where: Historical story · describing a winter journey
uses.sentence: A wan light fell across the fields as the weary travellers continued home.
uses.tip: It can describe a pale face, a faded look or a faint quality of light.

origin.summary: Old English wann meant pale or sallow. Its present sense developed through the idea of a person looking pale from illness or weakness.

timeline.text: Recorded as wann, meaning pale, sallow or lacking colour.
Widened to include weakness, exhaustion and a generally feeble appearance.
Mainly survives in literary descriptions of a pale or weak appearance.

cards.pitfall: This is a literary word, not a neutral everyday description; say pale or unwell when the tone is casual.

cards.meaning: To make a brief, involuntary face that shows pain, disgust, embarrassment, or sudden discomfort.
cards.nuance: A wince is usually a small reaction rather than a full-body movement. It can describe either a physical response or a figurative reaction to something unpleasant.

uses.where: Team meeting · hearing a risky proposal
uses.sentence: I winced when the budget estimate was mentioned.
uses.tip: Use the past tense when describing someone’s reaction to a person, idea, or event.

uses.sentence: She winced after accidentally swallowing a mouthful of chili sauce.
uses.tip: It fits brief reactions that show discomfort without adding much drama.

uses.sentence: He winced at the sight of the damaged equipment.
uses.tip: Use it to make a written reaction immediate and vivid.

origin.summary: From Old English wincian, meaning to turn, twist, or writhe. The modern sense developed into a brief movement or facial reaction caused by discomfort.

timeline.text: Wincian meant to turn, twist, or writhe.
Recorded in English for a twisting movement or expression of discomfort.
Usually describes a brief, involuntary grimace.

cards.pitfall: A wince is usually brief and involuntary; use flinch if the person moves away from something or recoil for a stronger backward movement.
